opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting case, because attention sinks are one of those phenomena that look strange from the activation side but start to make a lot more sense when you think in terms of parameters and mechanisms.

For anyone unfamiliar: an attention sink is when a head puts a large share of its attention on some token, often the beginning-of-sequence token or a delimiter, that doesn't seem to carry much useful information. The usual interpretation is that it's a kind of "no-op" default. Softmax forces attention to sum to one, so if a head has nothing useful to do on a given token, it needs somewhere to dump that attention mass, and the sink token's value vector is roughly harmless, maybe near zero or in a direction the downstream layers ignore.

In parameter decomposition, like the stochastic parameter decomposition work we've been doing, the goal is to break the network's weights into subcomponents, each implementing a piece of the computation, under the constraint that on any given input only a small number of them need to be active, or "causally important," to reproduce the output. So the natural question is: what does the sink look like in that picture?

My intuition is that the sink behavior should show up as its own fairly distinct mechanism, a subcomponent or a small set of them in the query-key weights that implement "attend to the sink by default." What's interesting is that this mechanism is active almost all the time, which sits awkwardly with the sparsity assumption we usually make. Most of our decompositions assume that any given mechanism is only needed on a small fraction of inputs. A sink is the opposite: it's a kind of always-on background mechanism, and the interesting computation is what happens when the head *departs* from it.

So I think it pushes you to think about the decomposition in a slightly different way. The sink component acts like a baseline, and the other, sparser components implement the conditions under which the head turns on and attends somewhere meaningful. In a sense, the head's "real" function is gating: does this context trigger me or not? The sink is what the head does when the answer is no.

That also has methodological implications. If you ablate the sink-related parameters naively, you can get big, misleading effects, because suddenly attention is spread across tokens the head was never supposed to read from. So when we measure causal importance, we have to be careful that we aren't just rediscovering "the softmax needs somewhere to go" and calling it a deep mechanism. Getting the decomposition to cleanly separate the default behavior from the input-specific behavior is a nice test of whether the method is carving the network at its actual joints.

More broadly, I see this as one of many cases where thinking in parameter space helps clarify things. In activation space, you see a giant spike of attention and huge norms on certain tokens and it looks bizarre. In mechanism space, it looks like a pretty sensible design: a default component plus a set of conditional components that override it. I think that framing will generalize to a lot of other "weird" phenomena, like massive activations, that look pathological until you ask what computational role the parameters are playing.

r001.rationale: The response asks what attention-sink behavior would look like in parameter decomposition and proposes it could appear as a distinct, mostly always-on subcomponent—a semantic equivalent of asking whether a “junk sink” analogue could arise.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's an interesting connection, and I should say up front that attention sinks weren't something we set out to study. They're something that fell out of the decomposition when we looked at what the subcomponents were actually doing.

So for context, the thing we're trying to do with parameter decomposition, and APD before it, and now SPD, is take a network's parameters and break them into a set of components where each component is, ideally, a mechanism. Something the network uses to do a particular piece of computation. And the criterion we use is roughly: can you reconstruct the network's behavior on any given input using only a small number of these components? So you want faithfulness, you want them to sum back to the original weights, and you want minimality, you want as few of them active as possible on each datapoint.

Now, the attention sink phenomenon is this thing where a lot of attention heads, when they don't have anything useful to attend to, dump their attention onto the first token, or the BOS token, or some other fixed position. It's basically a "do nothing" operation. The head has to put its attention mass somewhere because softmax sums to one, so it parks it on a token whose value vector contributes roughly nothing.

Where this becomes relevant to decomposition is that if you take the view that a mechanism is something that's used to perform a function, the attention sink is a mechanism in a slightly degenerate sense. It's the mechanism for "this head is off right now." And when you decompose the query and key weights of a head, you often find that there's a component, or a small number of components, that's essentially dedicated to that. It's active on a very large fraction of inputs, it's low rank, and what it's doing is producing a query that matches the key of the sink position.

That's actually a nice sanity check for the method, because it's exactly the kind of thing you'd expect to be cleanly separable. It's a function that's almost orthogonal to the rest of what the head does. But it also raises a question about how you count it. If you're using minimality, the number of components active per datapoint, and you have a component that's active essentially always, then it's sort of a background term. You could argue it should be absorbed into a bias-like component, or that it should be thought of as part of the default state of the network rather than as a mechanism per se.

The deeper thing I'd point at is that attention sinks are a symptom of a more general issue, which is that networks don't always have a clean "null" operation available, and they build one out of whatever's lying around. And decomposition methods have to be robust to that. If your method assumes that every component corresponds to some semantically meaningful feature of the input, you'll get confused by things like sinks, which correspond to the absence of a feature. So I think of it as one of a class of things, along with things like norm-regulating directions and position-tracking components, where the network is doing bookkeeping rather than computation, and a good decomposition should isolate the bookkeeping rather than smearing it across the components that are doing the actual work.

So the short version is: attention sinks show up as their own components, that's encouraging, and the fact that they show up tells you something about what kind of object a "mechanism" is. It's not always an interesting feature detector. Sometimes it's just the network's way of standing still.

r001.rationale: The response explains how attention sinks appear as components in parameter decomposition, but it does not ask whether an analogous “junk sink” could arise.

astra-6.text:
I think the connection is that we shouldn’t expect every parameter subcomponent to correspond to a clean, human-interpretable concept. Some components might play a more mechanical role, and an attention sink is a useful example of that.

With attention, you’ve got a distribution of weights that has to sum to one. But sometimes there isn’t anything useful for a head to attend to. An attention sink gives it somewhere to put that weight without necessarily contributing much useful information. So if you’re decomposing the network’s parameters, you might find a component whose role is to implement that behavior, rather than to represent something like a particular topic or feature.

And that changes how you’d evaluate the decomposition. A component that looks semantically uninteresting could still be important to how the network works. You’d want to intervene on it and ask whether it actually provides that sink behavior, and how removing it affects the other components. The goal is to recover the mechanisms, including the mundane bookkeeping, rather than assume that every piece will have a nice conceptual label.

r001.rationale: It says a parameter subcomponent might implement attention-sink behavior as a mechanical role, expressing that a sink-like analogue could appear in the decomposition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the attention sink is a useful example of why decomposing a network into parameter subcomponents is subtle. You might look at an attention head and say, “This head moves information from one token to another.” But sometimes it needs to do nothing. And because the attention weights have to sum to one, doing nothing can involve attending to a token whose value has very little effect on the output. That token acts as an attention sink.

So the behavior you care about might depend both on a component that routes useful information and on a component that provides somewhere to put attention when that information isn’t needed. Those can look like separate mechanisms in parameter space, even though they work together functionally.

For me, the implication is that we shouldn’t expect every parameter subcomponent to have a neat, standalone semantic interpretation. Some components may provide infrastructure that allows other components to operate. And if we want a faithful decomposition, we need to capture those interactions, rather than just identify pieces that look meaningful in isolation.

r001.rationale: The response explains how attention sinks may function as infrastructure in a decomposition, but it does not ask whether an analogous “junk sink” could arise.
